points.en: The four tasks in order are summary, confirmation, prayer and release.
The order is intentional: summary makes the work clear and nameable, confirmation fixes the commitment, prayer entrusts it to God, and release sends the counselee out.
The prayer thanks God for the session and asks His strength for the action ahead, for this wife's conversation with her son.
It prays for the counselee by name and for the person the action will affect, here the son.
It commits the outcome, whatever it proves to be, into God's sovereign hands.
The counselee is invited to pray herself, since her own prayer places her commitment before God.
Refusing to release fosters dependency the counselee should have outgrown, since counseling aims at his capacity to live without the counselor.
It can reveal the counselor's own need to be needed, turning ministry into self-service, and may displace Christ as the one the counselee depends on.
The claim is wrong because closure is itself ministry and the goal is the counselee's restored capacity to live without the counselor; an unending case fosters dependency.
True compassion gives focused help for a season and then releases the counselee with affection, leaving the door open without tethering him.
A finite counselor cannot be indefinitely available without cost to himself and his family.
The summary shows counseling as purposeful work and the confirmation shows the counselee as a responsible agent who must own a concrete obedience.
The prayer shows the work finally belongs to God, and the release shows the counselor as a finite servant to whom the person is entrusted only for a season.
Take the fear seriously without undoing closure or fostering dependence: remind the counselee of the work done and the concrete plan already prepared.
Release warmly with assurance that the Lord goes with him and a clear way to return if needed, rather than either abandonment or endless availability.
James 5:16 joins confession with mutual prayer for healing; closing prayer commits the counseling work and the next action to God.
Prayer is indispensable rather than a ritual ending: ask God's strength, entrust the outcome to Him and, where appropriate, invite the counselee to pray.
Releasing too soon abandons unfinished work and a half-prepared plan; complete and confirm the work before ending.
Releasing too late fosters dependence; when the counselee is equipped, release warmly with a clear route back if help is needed.
The Lord present in the counseling room remains with the counselee afterward, so release is not abandonment.
Closure sends the counselee out equipped and accountable, trusting God's continuing care rather than dependence on the counselor.
The parting words are warm and confident, affirming the counselee's capacity and that the Lord goes with him.
They release him without possessiveness: the door stays open, but he is told he does not need the counselor to do what he is equipped to do.
They locate his sufficiency in the Lord rather than in the counselor's continued presence.
